name: Ursa Major
introduction: is the Great Bear, the third-largest constellation, though most people know only part of it: the seven bright stars of the Big Dipper, also called the Plough. North of about 41° latitude the Dipper never sets, wheeling around the pole every night, high in spring evenings and low in autumn.

sections.title: What makes it special
paragraphs: Five of the Dipper’s seven stars, [Merak](hip:53910), [Phecda](hip:58001), [Megrez](hip:59774), [Alioth](hip:62956) and [Mizar](hip:65378), are siblings. They belong to the Ursa Major Moving Group, stars born together a few hundred million years ago that still drift through space side by side, about 80 light-years from us. This is one of the nearest star clusters to the Sun.

The two ends of the Dipper are not part of the family. [Dubhe](hip:54061) and [Alkaid](hip:67301) move in different directions, so over the next hundred thousand years the familiar shape will slowly bend out of recognition.

The Dipper is also the northern sky’s best guide. A line from Merak through Dubhe, extended about five times, reaches Polaris. Follow the curve of the handle instead to “arc to Arcturus”, the bright orange star of Boötes.

sections.title: Notable stars
paragraphs: [Mizar](hip:65378), at the bend of the handle, has a fainter neighbor, Alcor, that sharp eyes can separate; the pair has been called the horse and rider and used as an eyesight test. Through a telescope, Mizar itself splits into two. It was among the first double stars seen through a telescope, the first photographed, and the first found to be a spectroscopic binary. Altogether, Mizar and Alcor contain six stars.

[Dubhe](hip:54061), the top of the bowl, is an orange giant about 120 light-years away, the odd-colored star among the Dipper’s white ones. [Alioth](hip:62956) is the brightest star of the constellation, and [Megrez](hip:59774), the faintest of the seven, joins the handle to the bowl. [Alkaid](hip:67301), at the end of the handle, is a hot blue-white star about 100 light-years away.

sections.title: Beyond the stars
paragraphs: Away from the plane of the Milky Way, Ursa Major opens a clear view into deep space. Its galaxies include the pair M81 and M82, about 12 million light-years away, where gravitational interaction has triggered a burst of star formation in M82, and the face-on Pinwheel Galaxy, M101. Closer to home, the Owl Nebula, M97, is the glowing shell of a dying star.

Among the nearest stars, the red dwarf [Lalande 21185](id:lalande-21185), about 8 light-years away, also lies within the Great Bear’s boundaries, though it is far too faint to see without a telescope.
